themeName: Theme 3: Business Behaviour and the Labour Market

cards.front: Why do firms grow — and why do some stay small?
cards.back:
The underlying incentive is profit. Growth brings economies of scale, market power over prices and suppliers, easier access to finance, and stronger brand recognition.

Firms stay small because of diseconomies of scale, market conditions (niche or fiercely competitive markets), or owner preference — keeping control and a manageable lifestyle over expansion.

cards.front: Explain the principal-agent problem and the divorce of ownership and control.
cards.back:
In large firms the owners (shareholders) do not run the business — managers do. This separation of ownership and control means managers may pursue their own objectives — higher salaries, sales maximisation, perks — instead of the owners' goal of profit maximisation.

Solutions align incentives: performance-related pay, bonuses and stock options that make managers gain when shareholders do.

cards.front: Distinguish public from private sector, and profit from not-for-profit organisations.
cards.back:
Public sector — owned and funded by the government, usually to provide services in the public interest (the NHS). Private sector — owned by individuals or shareholders, usually profit-motivated.

Profit organisations aim to generate financial returns for owners; not-for-profit organisations, such as charities, reinvest any surplus in their social purpose instead.

cards.front: Distinguish organic from inorganic growth.
cards.back:
Organic growth is growth generated from within the business using its own resources — new products, new locations, more market share. Slower, but controlled.

Inorganic growth is growth achieved through mergers or takeovers of other businesses — faster, but riskier: integration can fail, cultures can clash, and the price paid may exceed the value gained.

cards.front: Distinguish horizontal, vertical and conglomerate integration.
cards.back:
Horizontal — merging with a competitor at the same stage of production (two car manufacturers), raising market share. Vertical — merging along the supply chain: backward with a supplier (a car maker buying a tyre maker) to secure inputs; forward with a distributor to secure outlets and margin.

Conglomerate — merging with an unrelated business, spreading risk across markets.

cards.front: What constrains business growth?
cards.back:
Market size — niche or saturated markets cap expansion, pushing firms to internationalise. Access to finance — smaller firms look riskier, so borrowing is harder and dearer. Owner objectives — lifestyle goals or satisficing over rapid growth.

Regulation — competition policy (the CMA) can block mergers that create too much market power, and rules on demerit goods can cap whole markets.

cards.front: What is a demerger, and why do firms demerge?
cards.back:
A demerger is when a large firm splits into two or more separate, independent businesses — the opposite of a merger.

Reasons: reduce diseconomies of scale; increase focus on the core business; resolve culture clashes from an earlier merger; shed loss-making divisions; raise capital; or regulatory pressure — the CMA can force a demerger to cut monopoly power.

cards.front: Evaluate the impacts of a demerger on the business, workers and consumers.
cards.back:
Business — lower average costs and sharper focus, against transition costs and lost synergies. Workers — better conditions and career paths in focused firms, against redundancies and transition uncertainty.

Consumers — more competition can mean lower prices and better service; but smaller firms may lose scale economies, which can push costs and prices the other way.

cards.front: Name the four business objectives in the Edexcel specification, with their rules.
cards.back:
Profit maximisation — the traditional assumption, maximising shareholder returns: produce where MC = MR. Revenue maximisation — for market share or scale economies: MR = 0. Sales maximisation — grow volume while breaking even: AC = AR.

Satisficing — a satisfactory rather than maximum profit, balancing shareholders against managers' own objectives (the principal-agent problem); output and price lie between the profit-max and sales-max positions.

cards.front: Show profit maximisation on a firm diagram.
cards.back:
Profit is maximised at the output Q where MC = MR: below Q each extra unit adds more revenue than cost; beyond Q it adds more cost than revenue.

Read the price P off the AR curve at Q and average cost C off the AC curve — with P above C, the gap times Q is supernormal profit.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with the profit-maximising point marked where MC crosses MR at output Q, price P read from AR and average cost C from AC

cards.front: Show revenue maximisation on a firm diagram.
cards.back:
Total revenue is maximised at the output where MR = 0 — the point where MR crosses the quantity axis. Up to Q every unit still adds revenue; beyond it, MR is negative and revenue falls.

Firms may choose this to build market share or reach scale economies — output is higher and price lower than at profit max, and profit is sacrificed while revenue peaks.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with the revenue-maximising point marked where MR crosses the quantity axis at output Q, price P read from AR

cards.front: Show sales maximisation on a firm diagram.
cards.back:
The largest output a firm can sell without making a loss is where AC = AR: price just equals average cost, so the firm breaks even and earns only normal profit.

Motives: market share, clearing stock, or limit pricing — a price too low for potential entrants to match profitably. Output is the highest of the three objectives, price the lowest.
cards.svgAlt: Firm diagram with the sales-maximising point marked where AC crosses AR at output Q, with price equal to average cost

cards.front: Why might a firm satisfice rather than maximise profit?
cards.back:
Because of the principal-agent problem: managers may prefer higher salaries, job security or perks, and choose a profit level acceptable to shareholders while meeting their own goals. In small firms, owners may satisfice to protect work-life balance.

On the diagram, a satisficing firm's output and price sit between the profit-maximising and sales-maximising positions — enough profit to satisfy, not the maximum available.

cards.front: Define and give the formulas for total, average and marginal revenue.
cards.back: TR = P × Q, the firm's total earnings from sales. AR = TR ÷ Q — which simplifies to the price per unit, so the AR curve is the firm's demand curve. MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ, the additional revenue from selling one more unit.
cards.formulaHtml: TR=P×Q;AR=TR/Q;MR=ΔTR/ΔQTR = P × Q; AR = TR/Q; MR = ΔTR/ΔQTR=P×Q;AR=TR/Q;MR=ΔTR/ΔQ

cards.front: Show the revenue curves in perfect competition.
cards.back:
Firms are price takers, selling every unit at the market price, so demand is perfectly elastic: D = AR = MR = P, one horizontal line.

With price fixed, total revenue rises at a constant rate — a straight ray from the origin.
cards.svgAlt: Horizontal line at price P labelled D=AR=MR=P, with a straight total revenue ray rising from the origin

cards.front: Show the revenue curves in imperfect competition.
cards.back:
Firms are price makers but must cut price to sell more, so AR (the demand curve) slopes down and MR lies below AR — in a linear diagram, twice as steep.

TR therefore rises at a decreasing rate, peaks exactly where MR = 0 (quantity Q), and falls beyond it as MR turns negative.
cards.svgAlt: Downward-sloping AR with a steeper MR crossing the quantity axis at Q, and a total revenue curve peaking directly above Q

cards.front: State the total revenue rule linking PED to pricing decisions.
cards.back:
If demand is price elastic (PED > 1), cutting price raises TR and raising price lowers it. If demand is price inelastic (PED < 1), raising price raises TR. At unitary elasticity (PED = 1), price changes leave TR unchanged.

On the imperfect-competition diagram: demand is elastic above the TR peak, inelastic beyond it — MR = 0 marks the boundary.

cards.front: Define the seven cost measures in the specification.
cards.back:
Fixed costs do not vary with output (rent, salaries); variable costs vary directly with it (raw materials, hourly wages). TC = TFC + TVC.

The averages divide by output: AC = TC ÷ Q, AFC = TFC ÷ Q, AVC = TVC ÷ Q. MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ — the additional cost of producing one more unit.
cards.formulaHtml: TC=TFC+TVC;AC=TC/Q;MC=ΔTC/ΔQTC = TFC + TVC; AC = TC/Q; MC = ΔTC/ΔQTC=TFC+TVC;AC=TC/Q;MC=ΔTC/ΔQ

cards.front: A firm has fixed costs of £200. Variable costs are £80 at 10 units, £140 at 20, £250 at 30 and £400 at 40. Calculate TC and AC at each output, and MC between each step.
cards.back:
TC = 200 + TVC: 280, 340, 450, 600

AC = TC ÷ Q: 280 ÷ 10 = £28; 340 ÷ 20 = £17; 450 ÷ 30 = £15; 600 ÷ 40 = £15

MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ: (340 − 280) ÷ 10 = £6; then £11; then £15

Note where AC stops falling: between 30 and 40 units MC equals AC at £15 — average cost bottoms out exactly where marginal cost catches it.

cards.front: Draw the short-run cost curves, and explain their shapes.
cards.back:
Diminishing marginal productivity shapes them all: with at least one factor fixed, extra workers eventually add less and less output, so MC falls briefly then rises — and the average curves are U-shaped.

MC cuts both AVC and AC at their minimum points: while MC is below an average it drags it down, once above it pulls it up. AFC falls continuously as fixed costs spread over more units.
cards.svgAlt: J-shaped MC curve cutting the AVC and AC curves at their minimum points, with AFC falling continuously

cards.front: Show the relationship between short-run and long-run average cost curves.
cards.back:
Each SRAC curve represents one scale of plant — fixed in the short run. In the long run all factors are variable, so the firm can choose any plant size: the LRAC is the envelope of the SRAC curves, touching each from below.

Moving down the LRAC means growing onto bigger, cheaper plants (economies of scale); beyond the minimum, further scale raises average costs.
cards.svgAlt: U-shaped LRAC curve as the envelope of three short-run average cost curves, with SRAC2 touching at the LRAC minimum

cards.front: Name the six types of internal economies of scale.
cards.back:
Purchasing — bulk-buying discounts; technical — large-scale machinery affordable only at volume; managerial — specialist managers; financial — cheaper borrowing as lenders see less risk; marketing — advertising spread over more units; risk-bearing — diversification across products and markets.

All are reasons within the business why average costs fall as output grows — they drive the LRAC's falling section.

cards.front: Show economies and diseconomies of scale on the LRAC curve, and mark the MES.
cards.back:
The falling section is economies of scale; the rising section is diseconomies, where size breeds bureaucracy, communication failures and weaker coordination.

The minimum efficient scale is the lowest output at which the lowest possible long-run average cost is reached — the bottom of the curve. Its position matters for market structure: a high MES leaves room for only a few efficient firms.
cards.svgAlt: U-shaped LRAC curve with the economies-of-scale section falling, diseconomies rising, and the minimum efficient scale marked at the bottom

cards.front: Distinguish internal from external economies of scale.
cards.back:
Internal economies arise within the business — its own scale lowers its own average costs (purchasing power, technical scale, and the rest).

External economies arise outside the business: the whole industry's growth lowers costs for every firm in it — a skilled local labour pool, specialist suppliers clustering nearby, shared infrastructure. Internal economies move a firm along its LRAC; external economies shift the whole curve down.

cards.front: Why do diseconomies of scale set in?
cards.back:
Size itself becomes the cost driver: communication stretches across more layers and sites; coordination and control weaken as management grows remote from operations; motivation falls when workers feel like small parts of a vast machine; and bureaucracy multiplies.

This is why growth is not automatically profitable — and why some firms demerge to get back below the point where average costs turn upward.
